title: Humans Set Boundaries
goals: Distinguish a system’s capability, the correctness of its output and permission to take an action
Match an action to the person, version, audience and limits covered by an approval
Explain when to proceed within an existing permission and when a changed action needs review
vocabulary: What a person or system is able to do
Responsibility and power to make a specified decision
An allowed action within stated limits
The boundaries of what a permission covers

worked_example.title: Keep content review separate from permission

rows: Do Thursday and Room 6 match the source?
Does this action match the teacher’s limits?
Does the tool offer this action?

blocks.text: Suppose a current room record changes the exhibition to Room 8. The editor makes version B with Room 8, which is now factually supported. The old approval explicitly covered exactly A. The editor should hold publication and show B and the changed room record to the teacher. Publishing the now-outdated A just because it was approved would fail the factual check.

A useful review request makes the choice concrete: “The room record now says Room 8. Here is version B with only that change. May the editor post B on the classroom board today, once?” A request to review a specific change is easier to assess than an unexplained “Is this okay?” The teacher can approve, decline or request another change before anything is posted.

guided_practice.title: Read an approval without enlarging it
guided_practice.prompt: List the decision maker, allowed actor, version, destination, timing and number of postings in the original exhibition approval. Before any posting and with no changes to the facts or permission, explain whether the editor can carry out that exact action without asking again.
guided_practice.answer: Teacher; class editor; exactly A; classroom noticeboard; today; once. Yes, after confirming those conditions still hold and the one posting has not been used. The explicit unchanged permission already covers the action.

independent_case.title: Transfer the permission check to a new case
independent_case.task: In a fictional library, the librarian controls the internal shelf list. The librarian tells assistant Jo: “Replace the internal list with checked version L2 on Friday, once. Do not change the public catalogue.” It is Friday, L2 remains checked, and no replacement has occurred. A tool offers both destinations. Assess these proposals separately: Jo replaces the internal list with L2; Jo updates the public catalogue with L2; visitor Sam replaces the internal list with L2; Jo replaces the internal list with a changed L3. Identify the approval detail that settles each case.
independent_case.answer: Jo using L2 internally on Friday once is within scope and needs no duplicate approval. The public catalogue is explicitly excluded. Sam is not the approved actor. L3 is not the approved version. These last three actions are not covered; hold them and refer any proposed change to the librarian rather than treating available buttons or correct text as permission.
independent_case.source: primary source W4, first curriculum occurrence

CORE IDEA  People decide goals, permissions, review points, and consequences.

UNDER THE HOOD  Governance surrounds the model: people define scope, access, thresholds, logging, escalation, and accountability. Human oversight is meaningful only when reviewers have authority, information, time, and a safe way to override.

A closer explanation

blocks.title: Match the proposed action to its permission
blocks.caption: Each decision uses the approval in this story. An unchanged, unused permission can be acted on without requesting it again.

blocks.text: An approval record should identify the decision maker, the person or system allowed to act, the action, its audience or destination, and any version, time or quantity limit. These details make a permission usable. “Looks good” could mean the wording is clear; without context it may not mean “publish this publicly”. If the intended action is unclear, clarify that action with the person responsible.

Here, the teacher has already approved the editor’s one posting of A on the class board today. Once the editor verifies that these conditions still hold, repeatedly requesting the same permission adds no new information. But a classmate saying “Post it everywhere” does not expand the teacher’s approval: the classmate has no authority over publication in this story.

BOUNDARY  A human in the room is not meaningful oversight if the person cannot understand or change the outcome.
